lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children's voices can change the world. Birimo's glowing map leads us, with Ms. Emma, to a small research harbor by the sea. There, we meet Dr. Marina Vale, a kind ocean scientist with a silver diving watch. She points to a little round submarine with thick round windows and bright lamps. This is the Bluebell, she says. I'm the pilot, so you're safe with me. Down we go! Through the porthole, the water turns from light blue to dark blue, and then to black. Dr. Vale says, Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. Kiko whispers, This is the place where light never reaches. Say it with me. This is the place where light never reaches. Wonderful! Then soft blue lights appear below us. Let's read the welcome sign at the city gate. "Welcome to Deep Sea City! You are now 3,800 meters under the sea. Our city is made of glass domes, and tunnels join them together. Every dome is full of fresh air, so you can walk and breathe just like at home. Visit the gardens under our blue lamps, the Research Center, the Coral Library, and the aquarium hall with its big windows. In the Coral Library, you can find books about almost every creature in the sea. In the middle stands the Great Dome, the biggest dome of all. Please stay with your group and enjoy your visit. Our guides are always happy to help!" How deep is Deep Sea City? 3,800 meters. What is inside every dome? Fresh air. A little lanternfish with glowing blue spots swims up in a water tunnel next to us. Her voice comes from a shell speaker. Hi! I'm Lumi! She is carrying a glass lamp with six empty pearl holders. This is the Lamp of Knowledge, Lumi says. In one month, we will hold our Research Festival in the Great Dome, and young researchers will present what they found. When you learn a new research skill, a glowing pearl will appear in the lamp. Let's find out! Now, phonics. Bio means life. Biology is the study of living things. A biography is a book about someone's life. A biome is a large area with its own climate, plants and animals. The deep sea is a biome, too! Next time, we'll visit the aquarium hall and see creatures that glow.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This is the place where light never reaches. Today, Lumi takes us to the aquarium hall with Ms. Emma and Dr. Vale. The hall has huge windows that look out into the deep sea. Dr. Vale turns off the room lights, and we wait quietly. At first, everything is black. Then, little by little, we see tiny lights. Blue lights, green lights, and lights that blink on and off! Riko whispers, No way! Where is that light coming from? Dr. Vale smiles and says, The animals are making it. Many deep-sea animals make their own light. Scientists call this bioluminescence. Haru tries to say the long word, and everyone laughs. Then Kiko says it in a simple way. Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Say it with me. Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Excellent! Let's read the sign next to the big window. "Lights in the Dark. Down here, there is no sunlight, but you can still see tiny lights. Many deep-sea animals make their own light. Scientists call this bioluminescence. Why do they glow? Some use light to find food. Some use it to hide, and some use it to talk to each other. Others flash to scare away enemies. Look at the anglerfish in Window 3. Some anglerfish have a glowing lure on their head. The light attracts small fish, and then, gulp! Now look at Window 5. These small fish are lanternfish. Their glowing spots shine like tiny stars. There are huge numbers of lanternfish in the ocean. Please do not tap on the glass." Why do some animals glow? To find food, to hide, to talk to each other, or to scare away enemies. What does the anglerfish's lure do? It attracts small fish. Lumi swims next to the window and blinks her blue spots. Now you know my secret! I'm a lanternfish, too! Now, phonics. Bio means life. Bioluminescent means making your own light. It's bio plus luminescent, which means giving light. Lanternfish are bioluminescent. Biodiversity means the variety of living things. The deep sea has amazing biodiversity. The biosphere is all the parts of the Earth where life exists, from the highest mountains to the deepest sea. Next time, we'll find out why the deep sea is so dark.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Today, Dr. Vale takes us to the observation room in the Research Center. On the wall, there is a tall chart of the ocean, from the surface all the way down to the seafloor. At the top, it is bright blue. In the middle, it gets darker. At the bottom, it is black. Birimo looks out the window and asks, Why is it so dark out there? Did somebody turn off the sea? Everyone laughs. Haru guesses, Maybe the water is dirty? Dr. Vale shakes her head. Sunlight comes from above, and the water slowly takes it away. So the deeper you go, the less light there is. Then Haru says it clearly. The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Say it with me. The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Perfect! Let's read the depth chart. "How Deep Does Light Go? From the surface to about 200 meters: Sunlight reaches well only this top part of the ocean. This is the bright part, where the water looks blue. From 200 meters to 1,000 meters: The water gets darker and darker as you go down. Below about 1,000 meters: It is completely dark. Scientists call this the midnight zone, because it is like night all the time. The water down here is very cold, about 2 to 4 degrees. The deepest known place in the ocean is in the Mariana Trench, about 11,000 meters deep. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there is still a lot to find out." How far does sunlight reach well? About 200 meters. How cold is the deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees. Kiko points to the bottom of the chart. And we are here, at 3,800 meters! Lumi says, That's why my blue spots are so useful! Now, phonics. Bio means life. A biographer is a person who writes biographies, books about someone's life. An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria. Anti means against. Biodegradable means it can be broken down by tiny living things called bacteria. Banana peels are biodegradable. Next time, we'll learn about the strong push of the deep water.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Today, Dr. Vale shows us something we cannot see: pressure. She asks us to put our hands together and push. Push harder! Harder! That's pressure. Water is heavy, and the deeper you go, the more water there is above you. So the water pushes harder and harder. Riko looks a little worried. Is the Bluebell okay? Dr. Vale laughs kindly. Don't worry. The Bluebell and the domes of Deep Sea City are built to be very, very strong. Then Kiko asks, But what about the fish outside? They don't have strong walls! Dr. Vale opens a big research card and says, That's the amazing part. Deep-sea animals have special bodies. Say it with me. Deep-sea animals have special bodies. Great job! Let's read the research card. "Life Under Pressure. As you go deeper, the water pushes harder. Every 10 meters adds about the same push as all the air above us. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. So how do deep-sea animals live here? First, many of them have soft, jelly-like bodies. Second, many of them have no air sacs inside. Air can be squeezed, so without air sacs, the pressure doesn't crush them. Some animals also have very big eyes to catch tiny bits of light. And look at the dumbo octopus! Its fins look like big ears. Deep-sea bodies are just right for deep-sea life." How much harder does the water push at 4,000 meters? About 400 times harder than at the surface. Why do some animals have very big eyes? To catch tiny bits of light. Birimo flaps his hands next to his head and says, Look! I'm a dumbo octopus! Lumi giggles in her water tunnel. Now, phonics. Bio means life. Symbiosis is when two living things help each other. Sym means together. Biomimicry means copying nature's ideas to make inventions. Mimic means copy. Maybe someday, people will design new submarines by copying deep-sea animals! Biofuel is fuel made from plants. Next time, it's our Deep Sea Wonder Talk, and each of you will share one amazing fact.

Kiko says the first two questions out loud. Who wrote it? When was it written? Say it with me. Who wrote it? When was it written? Super! Let's read the web page Birimo found. "Fishy Fun Facts Page! We know everything about the ocean, so you never need to read a book again! Click here for more crazy facts! Click here to win a free submarine! Author: not shown. Date: not shown. Sources: none. Share this page with all your friends!" What does the web page say about anglerfish? They are as big as buses. Who wrote it? We don't know. There is no author and no date. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This article is about marine snow. It says that tiny bits of food fall like snow. It shows how deep-sea animals get food. Today, Dr. Vale gives a short talk at the Research Center, and Kiko is very excited, because the talk is about her research question: Why do some animals glow? Kiko opens her notebook and starts writing every single word. Dr. Vale talks, and Kiko writes, writes, writes. Oh no! Dr. Vale is already three sentences ahead! Ms. Emma whispers, Kiko, you don't need to write every word. Just write the keywords. Keywords are the most important words. Kiko tries again, and now her notes look like this. Take notes: glow, food, dark. Say it with me. Take notes: glow, food, dark. Super! Short words are quick to write, and later, they help you remember the whole idea. You can draw arrows between your keywords, too, and color the most important one with a highlighter. Let's read part of Dr. Vale's talk. "Why do some animals glow? Many deep-sea animals make their own light. We call this bioluminescence. But why do they do it? Scientists have found a few reasons. Some animals glow to find food. For example, some anglerfish use a glowing lure to attract small fish. Some animals use light to hide from their enemies. Some use light to talk to each other, a bit like flashing signals in the dark. And some make a sudden bright flash to scare enemies away. Remember, it is completely dark down here, so light is a very useful tool. And there may be more reasons that we haven't discovered yet." What are the four reasons? To find food, to hide, to talk to each other, and to scare enemies away. Which word did Kiko color with her highlighter? Glow, of course! Now, phonics. Let's practice pausing one more time. If you take notes, pause, you can remember more. Write short words, pause, not long sentences. The most important word in this paragraph, pause, is glow. After you read, pause, look at your notes again. Kiko holds up her notes and says, I can remember the whole talk now! Next time, Lumi has a fun challenge for us, and we'll need a sand timer!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Take notes: glow, food, dark. Today, Lumi has a surprise for us in the aquarium hall. Each of you has thirty seconds to tell us what you learned. Ready? Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Say it with me. Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Great! Let's read Lumi's challenge card. "The Summary Challenge. Step one: Look at your notes, not at a long page. Step two: When it's your turn, turn over the sand timer. Step three: Start with your topic, and then give the main point. You can use In short or The main point is. Step four: Give one or two details, not ten. Step five: Stop when the sand runs out. Everyone listens and cheers, and nobody laughs at mistakes. Remember, a good summary is short, clear and true. If you're not sure about a fact, say so. Don't forget to say where you found your facts. Breathe and smile before you start. Good luck, young researchers!" How long does each friend have? Thirty seconds. What should a good summary be? Short, clear and true. Riko goes first. In short, anglerfish use light to catch food. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Today, Lumi takes us to the Great Dome for the first time. It's huge! There are rows and rows of seats, a round stage, and a big screen. Lumi says, This is where the Research Festival will be. Young researchers from all over the city will stand right here At the festival, each of you will give a research talk about your own research question. Haru gulps. Here? In front of all those seats? Dr. Vale laughs kindly. Don't worry, Haru. Every good talk starts with a good opening, and an opening is easy to learn. First, say hello. Next, ask a fun question to wake up your listeners. Then, tell them your topic. Riko walks to the middle of the stage and tries it. Hello, everyone. Did you know that some fish make their own light? Today, I'd like to talk about the deep sea. Say it with me. Today, I'd like to talk about the deep sea. Great! Let's read the tips Dr. Vale wrote on the board. "How to Start a Great Talk. One: Walk to the middle of the stage, stand up straight, and smile. Two: Say hello to your listeners. Good morning, everyone! is a friendly way to start. Three: Ask a question or share a surprising fact. For example, ask, Have you ever seen a fish that glows? Or share a fact, like this one: below about 1,000 meters, the sea is completely dark. This makes your listeners curious. Four: Tell them your topic. Start with, Today, I'd like to talk about... Five: Breathe! The first ten seconds are the hardest. After that, it gets easier. Your listeners want you to do well!" What should you do after you say hello? Ask a question or share a surprising fact. Why? Because it makes your listeners curious. Birimo jumps onto the stage. At the festival, the four friends will begin with a short team talk called Three Things About the Deep Sea, and Haru is writing it. He has a great opening now, but the rest of his talk is a mess. He has twenty facts on one long page, and they're all mixed up! Back at the Research Center, Dr. Vale hands him a small stack of note cards. She says, Write one point on each card. Then put the cards in order. Three points are usually enough for a short talk. Haru picks his three best points and lines up the cards on the table. Then he practices with three helpful words: first, second and finally. First, the deep sea is dark. Second, it is cold. Finally, the pressure is strong. Say it with me. First, the deep sea is dark. Second, it is cold. Finally, the pressure is strong. Fantastic! These words are like signs on a path. They tell your listeners where they are in your talk. Let's read Haru's note cards. "Card one. First, the deep sea is dark. Sunlight reaches well only the top part of the ocean, about 200 meters. Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. Card two. Second, it is cold. Deep water is only about 2 to 4 degrees. Brr! Card three. Finally, the pressure is strong. Every 10 meters down adds about the same push as all the air above us. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. Many deep-sea animals have soft, jelly-like bodies, so the pressure doesn't crush them. That's also why the Bluebell has such thick walls and windows." How cold is deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees. How much harder does the water push at 4,000 meters? About 400 times harder. Kiko says, Your talk is so easy to follow now! Haru grins. And my giant squid facts can go in my own talk! Now, phonics. Ecology is the study of how living things and their homes are connected. An ecologist studies ecology. Technology means the tools and machines that people invent, like the Bluebell. Remember the strong part: e-COL-o-gy, e-COL-o-gist, tech-NOL-o-gy. Next time, we'll use pictures and a graph to make our talks even clearer!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, As you can see in this picture, the anglerfish has a glowing light. Today, Kiko practices her whole talk for Lumi in front of the big windows of the aquarium hall. Her opening is great, and her three points are clear. But at the very end, she just says, That's all. Bye! and runs off the stage. Lumi blinks her blue spots. Kiko, that was a bit sudden! A good talk needs a good ending, too. Ms. Emma explains that the ending of a talk is called the conclusion. In the conclusion, we say our main point again, so our listeners remember it. Then we can add a short message or a hope. We often start with two special words: in conclusion. Kiko thinks about her whole talk. What does she want everyone to remember? Then she says, In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Say it with me. In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Perfect! Let's read the new ending of Kiko's talk. "So why do some animals glow? Many deep-sea animals make their own light, and they use it in clever ways. Some glow to find food, some glow to hide, some use light to talk to each other, and some flash to scare enemies away. Before I started my research, I thought the deep sea was just dark and empty. Now I know that it is full of tiny lights, like stars in the night sky. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there may be glowing animals that nobody has seen yet. I hope you will keep asking questions about the ocean, too. In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Thank you!" What does Kiko say again in her ending? The four reasons why animals glow. What did Kiko think before her research? She thought the deep sea was just dark and empty. Lumi spins happily in her tunnel. That ending gave me goosebumps, and I'm a fish! Now, phonics. Meteorology is the study of weather. A meteorologist studies the weather and tells us if it will rain tomorrow. A volcanologist studies volcanoes, like Dr. Mori on the Island of Fire. Remember the strong part: me-te-or-OL-o-gy, me-te-or-OL-o-gist, vol-can-OL-o-gist. Next time, we'll have a big practice day in the Great Dome!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Speak slowly. Pause after each point. Today, we are back in the Research Center. Kiko gives her practice talk about why some animals glow. She speaks slowly and clearly, and everyone claps. Then Dr. Vale says, Now it's question time! Birimo raises his hand right away. Kiko, why is it so dark down here? Kiko's cheeks turn pink. She feels a little nervous. But Lumi swims up to the window and whispers through the shell speaker, Take a breath. You know this! When someone asks you a question, you can say something kind first. That gives you a moment to think. Then you can give your answer. That's a great question. Let me explain. Say it with me. That's a great question. Let me explain. Great! Let's read the card that Dr. Vale puts on the table. "How to Answer a Question. Listen to the whole question, and don't start talking too early. Look at the person who asked it, and smile. Say something kind, like That's a great question. Then say, Let me explain. Give a short answer first, and then add one reason or one example. For example, if someone asks why the deep sea is dark, you can say that sunlight only reaches the top 200 meters or so. Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. At the end, ask, Does that answer your question? Remember, a question is a gift. It shows that people were really listening to you." What should you do before you answer? lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That's a great question. Let me explain. Today, it's Riko's turn. She practices her talk about how deep-sea fish find food. She talks about big eyes, glowing lights and marine snow. Then Haru raises his hand. Riko, how cold is the water outside the dome? Riko stops. She didn't write that in her notes. What can she do? She doesn't want to make up a number. Lumi says, When you don't know for sure, be honest! Tell people what you think, and tell them you're not sure. So Riko takes a breath and makes a careful guess. I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Say it with me. I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Great! Then Riko asks Dr. Vale to check. Dr. Vale smiles and shows us a page from her science notebook. Let's read it. "Water Temperature in the Ocean. Near the surface, the water can be warm, especially in sunny places. But the deeper you go, the colder it gets. Deep water is very cold, about 2 to 4 degrees, even in hot parts of the world. Near the North and South Poles, sea water can be as cold as minus 2 degrees. But there are surprises on the seafloor, too. In some places, there are hot springs called hydrothermal vents. The water that comes out of them can be hotter than 350 degrees! Tube worms live near these vents, and they don't need any sunlight. The ocean is full of surprises, so a good researcher always checks the facts." How cold is deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees. What lives near hydrothermal vents? Tube worms. So Riko's guess was right! Dr. Vale says, Good job, Riko. You were honest, and you made a smart guess. Then you checked it. That's what real scientists do. Now, phonics. Let's read temperatures. −2°C is minus two degrees. 4°C is four degrees. 350°C is three hundred fifty degrees. We say one degree, but two degrees, with an s. Next time, we'll learn how to ask good questions, too!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Today, Haru gives his practice talk. His research question is, How big can giant squid grow? He shows a picture of a giant squid with its long arms and tentacles. He speaks slowly and pauses after each point. Everyone listens carefully. When Haru finishes, Ms. Emma says, Good listeners ask good questions. A good question starts with the topic, so the speaker knows what you want to ask about. Kiko raises her hand. I have a question about the giant squid. Say it with me. I have a question about the giant squid. Great! Let's read the question guide on the wall of the Research Center. "How to Ask a Good Question. First, listen to the whole talk. Write down one or two things you want to know more about. Wait until the speaker asks for questions, and then raise your hand. Start with the topic. For example, say, I have a question about the giant squid. Then ask one clear question, not three questions at once. Good questions often start with how, why, which or where. After the answer, say thank you. If you want to know more, you can ask a follow-up question. Remember, a good question helps everyone in the room learn something new, and that includes the speaker!" When should you raise your hand? When the speaker asks for questions. What words do good questions often start with? How, why, which or where. Kiko asks, How big are its eyes? Haru answers, They're as big as dinner plates, about 27 centimeters. Then Riko asks a follow-up question. Which are bigger, males or females? Haru says, Females are bigger. The biggest ones that scientists have measured are about 12 to 13 meters long. Now, phonics. Let's read lengths. 13 meters is thirteen meters. 27 cm is twenty-seven centimeters. 11 km is eleven kilometers. That's about how deep the Mariana Trench is! lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I have a question about the giant squid. Today, it's Birimo's turn. His research question is, Do deep-sea animals sleep? He explains that some fish seem to rest quietly, but scientists are still finding out. After his talk, Haru raises his hand. I have a question about lanternfish. Do lanternfish sleep, too? Birimo thinks and thinks. Hmm. I don't know yet. He doesn't want to guess this time. So he says, I'll look it up and tell you later. Say it with me. I'll look it up and tell you later. Great! It's a promise, so Birimo really has to do it. After lunch, he goes to the Coral Library with Ms. Emma. Mr. Oswin, the old sea turtle, pushes up his tiny reading glasses. Then he opens a big encyclopedia, very, very slowly. Check your sources! he says. Let's read the page. "Lanternfish. Lanternfish are small fish with glowing spots on their bodies. There are huge numbers of them in the ocean. In the daytime, many lanternfish stay deep down, where it is dark. At night, many of them swim up toward the surface to eat, and then they go back down again. Do lanternfish sleep? Scientists are still finding out. It is not easy to watch fish in the deep sea, because it is dark and very far away. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there are still many questions for young researchers to answer. Maybe you will be one of them!" What do many lanternfish do at night? They swim up toward the surface to eat. Do lanternfish sleep? Scientists are still finding out. The next morning, Birimo runs to Haru. I looked it up! Haru says, Really? What did you find out? Birimo tells him everything. He kept his promise! Now, phonics. Let's read numbers with units. 400 times is four hundred times. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. 3.8 km is three point eight kilometers. That's how deep Deep Sea City is! 100 km/h is one hundred kilometers per hour. Per means for each. Next time, Riko will be the host of a real question time!
